title: Desk Drawer Story Sequence Card Pack
audience: Families, homeschool groups, tutors, and adult-led writing tables for writers ages 7-11.
sessionLength: 16 printable story sequence cards plus adult guide tools, sequence routines, take-home sequence slips, and optional share prompts
safetyNote: No scary harm, no bullying, no romance, no weapons, no branded characters, no real child profiles.

cover.headline: Desk Drawer Story Sequence Card Pack
cover.subhead: Sixteen paper sequence cards turn pretend drawer objects into clear beginning-middle-ending story order.

beforeSession: Print and cut the desk drawer sequence cards before the writer arrives.
Choose six to ten cards for the group size and place the rest aside.
Set blank paper, pencils, blank slips, and a small envelope or box to stand in for the pretend drawer.
Explain that the drawer objects are fictional paper clues used to build a made-up story order.
Start with one adult example so writers see how beginning, middle, and ending cards line up.
paperSequenceSetup: Place the selected cards face down in a small envelope, tray, or pretend desk drawer.
Pull single cards and set each into one of three zones: beginning, middle, or ending.
Let writers move cards before writing so the sequence can change without erasing.
Keep blank bridge slips nearby for one missing event between two cards.
Save skipped cards in a later pile so the session keeps moving.
sequenceCoaching: Ask what has to happen before this card can make sense.
Use concrete transition words: first, next, then, after that, because, and finally.
When a writer stalls, offer two possible spots for the card and let the writer choose.
Point to the paper order before asking for another sentence.
Finish with one quick retell from left to right before the final writing round.
privacyAndSafetyNotes: Keep all work on paper and offline with the adult leader or family folder.
Use invented names, pretend places, and made-up drawer objects.
Redirect any personal or narrow real-life detail into a broad invented detail before writing.
A writer may point to one card or share one invented word instead of reading aloud.
Skip any prompt that stops feeling gentle, invented, paper-only, or adult-led.
familyHandoff: Send one ordered card row, one blank bridge slip, or one short fiction sentence.
Tell family adults the task is event order practice, not a mark of writing ability.
Invite one gentle paper retell using first, next, then, and finally.
Ask families to keep examples fictional and offline.
Return unfinished cards in a folder for the next adult-led session.
reset: Collect selected cards, blank slips, and draft pages.
Return finished pages to the writer or adult folder and recycle only scrap warm-ups.
Sort cards by beginning, middle, ending, cause, and transition focus if useful.
Shuffle the drawer stack before the next session.

sequenceRoutines.name: Drawer Pull Warm-Up
sequenceRoutines.bestFor: A gentle opening round for one writer or a small table.
steps: Pull three cards from the pretend drawer.
Read each card aloud and place them in any order.
Ask which card has to happen first.
Write one sentence for each card using first, next, and then.

sequenceRoutines.name: Beginning Middle Ending Sort
sequenceRoutines.bestFor: Writers who need a clear story structure before drafting.
steps: Draw six cards and spread them across the table.
Choose two cards for the beginning zone.
Choose two cards for the middle zone.
Choose two cards for the ending zone and retell the row aloud.

sequenceRoutines.name: Cause Card Chain
sequenceRoutines.bestFor: Practicing why one event leads to another.
steps: Pull four cards and choose one card to start the chain.
Place the next card only after saying what caused it.
Move any card that does not connect yet to a later spot.
Write the sequence as four short story beats.

sequenceRoutines.name: Missing Bridge Slip
sequenceRoutines.bestFor: Fixing a story that skips ahead too quickly.
steps: Read the ordered cards from left to right.
Stop where the story feels like it skipped a step.
Have the adult write one fictional bridge event on a blank slip.
Place the bridge slip in the gap and retell the sequence once.

sequenceRoutines.name: Setting Path Row
sequenceRoutines.bestFor: Showing how a character moves through a pretend drawer world.
steps: Pick three fictional drawer spots such as tab corner, paperclip hill, or stamp stack.
Place a card at each setting spot.
Decide which spot the character visits first, next, and last.
Write one sentence that shows the move between each spot.

sequenceRoutines.name: Ending Drawer Swap
sequenceRoutines.bestFor: Revising an ending without rewriting the full story.
steps: Keep the beginning and middle cards in their current order.
Pull two new ending cards from the pretend drawer.
Compare which ending fits the character's earlier choice.
Write the final two sentences using the chosen ending card.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: First Drawer Clue
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Pull three pretend drawer cards. Put the card that starts the made-up scene first, then write what ____________________ notices.
takeHomeSequenceSlips.familyLine: Family adult spots the beginning when ____________________ gives the story a clear first move.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Middle Bridge Slip
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Choose one card for the start and one for the end. Write the middle event that belongs between them: ____________________.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Last Card Close
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Choose a final pretend drawer object and write how the small story closes after ____________________.
takeHomeSequenceSlips.familyLine: The ending has arrived when ____________________ shows what changed last.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: First Next Finally Row
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Use three paper cards and write one First, one Next, and one Finally sentence about ____________________.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Because Drawer Chain
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Pick one paper drawer card that causes a change. Write what happens because ____________________ appears.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Tab Word Trail
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Write a three-sentence drawer story using after, then, and last. Put ____________________ in the sentence with your favorite transition word.
takeHomeSequenceSlips.familyLine: The transition word helps the listener understand where ____________________ belongs.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Numbered Label Strip
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Draw four paper label strips, number the events, and write which number belongs beside ____________________.
takeHomeSequenceSlips.familyLine: Check the event order by asking whether ____________________ happened before or after the other events.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Object Stack Sort
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Choose three fictional desk drawer objects. Arrange them by story job and explain why ____________________ goes in that spot.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Drawer Nook Path
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Draw three pretend spots inside a desk drawer scene. Show where ____________________ appears first, next, and last.
takeHomeSequenceSlips.familyLine: The setting sequence helps the listener follow how ____________________ moves through the pretend drawer world.

takeHomeSequenceSlips.title: Folded Note Fix
takeHomeSequenceSlips.direction: Make a small pretend drawer problem, then add two steps that lead to a gentle solution. Write the solution step for ____________________.
takeHomeSequenceSlips.familyLine: The problem-solution sequence works because ____________________ comes after the problem and helps close the story.
